article.title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19

extraction.summary: Full methodology for Nate Silver's FiveThirtyEight 2020 presidential forecast, which Silver says the 2024 Silver Bulletin model reproduces almost exactly, minus COVID-specific tweaks and the Cost of Voting Index. There are three steps. (1) Polling averages: a blend of a weighted average and a trend line, with likely-voter, house-effect and timeline adjustments, a convention bounce adjustment, and gradual credit for post-debate shifts. (2) Fundamentals: an 'enhanced snapshot' blending state polls with an ensemble of the rigid partisan-lean method, a demographic regression (up to 180 specifications) and a regional regression; then blending with an economic-index-and-incumbency prior on a published days-to-election weight schedule. (3) Uncertainty: national drift scaling with the cube root of days times an 8-component uncertainty index, Election Day error calibrated on polls since 1936 with fat tails, correlated state error over demographic and geographic variables, and state-specific error; 40,000 simulations covering 54 jurisdictions.

findings.statement: The 2020 FiveThirtyEight presidential model differs modestly from 2016: more uncertainty components (economic uncertainty, news volume); an economic index extended back to 1880, adjusted for partisanship and with an economic forecasting component; extra Election Day error for pandemic turnout; COVID severity and mail-vote share as covariance factors; half the usual convention bounce adjustment; revised polling averages; a Cost of Voting Index adjustment; event handling for debates; and a single version with no polls-only, polls-plus or now-cast.
findings.evidence_quote: We’re running only one version of the presidential model this year.

findings.statement: Polls in the 2020 presidential averages are weighted by sample size and pollster rating, and when one firm releases many polls each poll's weight is discounted so no pollster dominates.
findings.evidence_quote: if there are a large number of polls from one polling firm, the weight applied to each individual poll is discounted so no one pollster dominates the average.

findings.statement: The presidential polling averages blend a simple weighted average with a more aggressive trend-line method. Early in the campaign they rely mostly on the weighted average, and in the final weeks mostly on the trend line, so averages become more aggressive as Election Day nears.
findings.evidence_quote: So early on in the campaign, we rely mostly on the more conservative weighted average method, while in the final few weeks, we mostly use the trend line method

findings.statement: The 2020 likely-voter adjustment shifted registered-voter polls toward what LV polls would show. Historically Republicans gain under LV screens, mitigated when the Republican is an incumbent; in 2020 paired polls showed Trump gaining about 1 point in LV versions.
findings.evidence_quote: Generally speaking, this means that Republicans (such as Trump) gain ground relative to Democrats when applying a likely voter screen, although this effect is mitigated when the Republican is an incumbent.

findings.statement: The 2020 house-effects adjustment corrects polls that consistently lean toward a party or report more or fewer undecideds than others in the same state. Polls keep part of their house effect, since a small number of polls may reflect noise. House effects are computed mostly from polls of the same state, so a firm can lean differently in different states.
findings.evidence_quote: In calculating house effects, the model mostly uses polls from the same state, so a polling firm could theoretically have a Trump-leaning house effect in one state and a Biden-leaning house effect in another.

findings.statement: The timeline adjustment shifts older state polls for movement in the race since they were conducted, based on national polls and polls of similar states; for example, an older Arizona poll is shifted toward Trump if national and Nevada polls moved toward him.
findings.evidence_quote: Finally, we apply a timeline adjustment , which is based on a poll’s recency, and adjusts “old” polls for shifts in the overall race since it was conducted.

findings.statement: After major events such as debates, the forecast blends the post-event polling average with the pre-event average, moving fully to the post-event average only after a week or two depending on the event, because event-driven shifts often revert. Candidates must sustain post-event gains to get full credit.
findings.evidence_quote: After a week or two (depending on the event) though, the model will fully use the post-event polling average because it no longer necessarily expects a reversion to the mean.

findings.statement: At 2020 levels of polarization, the model expects a party to poll about 5 points better at the peak of its convention bounce, the day after its convention ends, fading fairly quickly, down from double-digit bounces in the past. In 2020 only half the usual adjustment was applied (virtual conventions) and back-to-back conventions largely cancelled: polls between the conventions were adjusted about 2 to 2.5 points toward Trump, and polls in the 2 to 3 weeks after the RNC less than 1 point toward Biden.
findings.evidence_quote: we would expect a party to poll about 5 percentage points better at the peak of its convention bounce on the day just after the conclusion of its convention

findings.statement: The 2020 partisan lean index weights the past two presidential elections relative to the nation at 75 percent for 2016 and 25 percent for 2012, so states that trended between them may revert somewhat to the mean.
findings.evidence_quote: In our partisan lean index, 75 percent of the weight is assigned to 2016 and 25 percent to 2012.

findings.statement: The partisan lean index includes a home-state adjustment for presidential and vice-presidential candidates. It is much larger for presidential candidates, larger in smaller states, and split when a candidate has two home states, e.g. Biden primary Delaware and secondary Pennsylvania, Trump primary New York and secondary Florida.
findings.evidence_quote: The size of the home-state adjustment is much larger for presidential candidates than for their running mates.

findings.statement: The partisan lean index also adjusts for state elasticity, using a blend of each state's elasticity in 2008, 2012 and 2016, and in 2020 for ease of voting via the Cost of Voting Index. The latter was removed in 2024.
findings.rationale: Lower voting barriers yield higher turnout and more Democratic votes empirically.
findings.evidence_quote: The elasticity scores we’re using for 2020 are based on a blend of each state's elasticity in 2008, 2012 and 2016.

findings.statement: The modeled state estimate is an ensemble of three methods. (1) The 'rigid method': the national margin, imputed mostly from state polls, plus the state's partisan lean, e.g. Biden +5 nationally plus D+10 lean gives Biden +15. (2) A demographic regression fitting current state polls on partisan lean plus combinations of race, income, education, urbanization, religiosity and a COVID severity index: up to 180 regressions with collinearity and size limits, averaged with weights by adjusted R-squared and every regression getting some weight. (3) A regional regression on partisan lean plus four region dummies. The rigid method, historically most accurate, gets the majority of the weight, then demographic, then regional.
findings.rationale: Infer what polls would say in sparsely polled states from better-polled ones.
findings.evidence_quote: The rigid method, which is the most accurate historically, receives the majority of the weight, followed by the demographic regression and then the regional regression.

findings.statement: The 'enhanced snapshot' for each state blends the state's polling average with the ensemble estimate, with poll weight depending on polling volume and recency. At the 2020 launch (Aug. 12) about 55 percent of the weight went to polls in the average state; in well-polled states near the end, as much as 97 to 98 percent. States without polls use the ensemble alone.

quantities.name: poll weight in average state at launch
poll weight late in well-polled states

findings.evidence_quote: As of the forecast launch (Aug. 12), around 55 percent of the weight goes to the polling average rather than to the ensemble in the average state.

findings.statement: National polls play relatively little role in the 2020 FiveThirtyEight presidential forecast beyond the trend-line adjustment. The national snapshot is the sum of the state snapshots weighted by projected turnout, based on population growth since 2016, voting-ease changes and current closeness, since closer states have higher turnout. National polls are not used in it.
findings.evidence_quote: National polls are not used in the national snapshot; it’s simply a summation of the snapshots in the 50 states and Washington, D.C.

findings.statement: The FiveThirtyEight economic index, used since 2012, has six variables: nonfarm payrolls (jobs), real personal consumption expenditures (spending), real disposable personal income (income), industrial production (manufacturing), CPI (inflation) and the S&P 500 (stock market). Each is standardized to roughly equal mean and standard deviation over data since 1946, measured over the two years before the election with much heavier weight on roughly the final six months, and calibrated on vintage real-time data where possible.
findings.rationale: Equal-weighted blend avoids p-hacking among many economic measures.
findings.evidence_quote: All variables are standardized so that they have roughly the same mean and standard deviation

findings.statement: The economic index is a z-score (0 is an average economy) extended approximately to 1880. Election Day values include 1932 -2.34, 1980 -1.71, 2008 -1.34, 1920 -1.52, 1936 +1.55, 1880 +1.37, 1984 +0.86, 1964 +0.70, 2012 -0.10 and 2016 +0.08. The economy explains only about 30 percent of the variation in incumbent-party performance.
findings.rationale: Expanding the sample matters even with less reliable early data.
findings.evidence_quote: In fact, we found that the economy explains only around 30 percent of the variation in the incumbent party’s performance

findings.statement: The 2020 fundamentals forecast also accounts for incumbency status: an elected incumbent (Trump 2020, Obama 2012), a successor incumbent (Ford 1976), or no incumbent (2008, 2016). It also accounts for polarization from House roll-call vote distance; greater polarization is associated with closer margins and smaller effects of the economy and incumbency.
findings.evidence_quote: Periods of greater polarization (such as today in the U.S.) are associated with closer electoral margins and also smaller impacts of economic conditions and incumbency.

findings.statement: The model forecasts each of the six economic variables to Election Day with some mean reversion, using recent stock market performance, which has some predictive power, and surveys of professional economists.
findings.rationale: Conditions at forecast time may not resemble November.
findings.evidence_quote: the model makes a simple forecast for each of the six economic variables, which accounts for some mean-reversion

findings.statement: Published schedule of weight on polls versus fundamentals by days until the election: 0 days 100/0; 5 days 97/3; 10 days 94/6; 25 days 89/11; 50 days 84/16; 75 days 79/21; 100 days 74/26; 150 days 65/35; 200 days 57/43; 250 days 47/53. At the 2020 launch it was 77/23. Fundamentals help the trailing side at the margin, and higher-elasticity states are shifted slightly more.
findings.rationale: Fundamentals have more misses once data before 1948 is included.

findings.statement: Silver considers fundamentals-only presidential models overrated: with many ways to measure the economy and few elections, it is easy to p-hack. Their telltale failure is fitting past elections well and predicting unknown ones poorly; one Q2-GDP model implied Biden would win nearly 1,000 electoral votes in 2020.
findings.evidence_quote: it’s easy to “p-hack” your way to glory with these models because there are so many ways to measure “the economy” but only a small sample size of elections

findings.statement: The 2020 model distinguishes four error types: national drift (change in the national forecast before Election Day), national Election Day error (final forecast miss), correlated state error along demographic or geographic lines, and state-specific error.
findings.evidence_quote: With that disclaimer out of the way, here are the four types of uncertainty that the model tries to account for:

findings.statement: National drift is calculated as Constant x (Days Until Election)^(1/3) x Uncertainty Index. The cube root implies polls do not become more accurate linearly but sharply toward the end.
findings.rationale: August is still early as far as polling goes.
findings.evidence_quote: Constant x (Days Until Election)^⅓ x Uncertainty Index

findings.statement: The FiveThirtyEight Uncertainty Index is an equally weighted blend of eight measures: (1) undecided share in national polls; (2) undecided plus third-party share; (3) polarization from House roll-call distance, which lowers uncertainty; (4) volatility of the national polling average; (5) volume of national polling; (6) gap between the polling snapshot and the fundamentals forecast; (7) standard deviation of the economic index components; (8) news volume, measured by full-width New York Times headlines over the past 500 days with recent days weighted more. In 2020 the overall level was about average relative to elections since 1972.
findings.rationale: With small samples and correlated measures, use an equal-weight blend rather than picking one or two metrics.
findings.evidence_quote: we think it is better to use an equally-weighted blend of all reasonable metrics rather than picking and choosing just one or two metrics.

findings.statement: National Election Day error uses a version of the uncertainty index that de-emphasizes components 6 to 8, which relate to future movement, and is calibrated on final-poll errors in elections since 1936 for sample size. Fat-tailed distributions are used for many error components, including Election Day error.
findings.rationale: Conservative given small samples; very accurate 2004-2012 polls may not be replicable.
findings.evidence_quote: the calculation is based on the error in final polls in elections since 1936 , rather than solely on more recent elections.

findings.statement: For 2020 the model increased national Election Day error, correlated state error and state-specific error by 20 percent, since pandemic primaries showed about 50 percent higher turnout variability and a 50 percent rise in turnout error is estimated to raise vote-share error by 20 percent. This COVID adjustment was removed in 2024.
findings.evidence_quote: we increase national Election Day error, correlated state error and state-specific error by 20 percent relative to their usual values

findings.statement: In each of 40,000 simulations per update, the model first draws national drift and national Election Day error and applies them roughly uniformly across states, scaled by elasticity. It then draws correlated state errors as random permutations over demographic and geographic variables, and finally residual state-specific error.
findings.evidence_quote: the model first picks two random numbers to reflect national drift (how much the national forecast could change) and national Election Day error

findings.statement: Correlated state error is simulated over these variables: race (white, Black, Hispanic, Asian); religion (evangelical, mainline Protestant, Catholic, Mormon, other, nonreligious); partisan lean in 2016 and 2012; latitude and longitude; region; urbanization; median household income; median age; gender; education (bachelor's share); immigration (share of the voting-eligible population); COVID severity; and expected mail-vote share. Most end-of-campaign state polling error is assumed correlated with other states.
findings.rationale: A Michigan miss is likely reflected in Wisconsin and Ohio.
findings.evidence_quote: we estimate that at the end of the campaign, most of the error associated with state polling is likely to be correlated with errors in other states.

findings.statement: States demographically resembling the nation have less polling error under correlated-error simulation, while outlier states are harder to predict; for example, underestimating Mormons barely affects national or Florida polls but could cause a huge miss in Utah.
findings.evidence_quote: states that are outliers based on some combination of the variables listed above tend to be harder to predict.

findings.statement: Residual state-specific error is relatively small and mainly a function of polling volume, larger in states with no polling, which is why unpolled Oregon had higher Trump odds than expected at the 2020 launch.
findings.evidence_quote: This tends to be relatively small, and is primarily a function of the volume of polling in each state, especially in states that have had no polling at all.

findings.statement: The presidential model forecasts 54 jurisdictions: 48 states, DC, Maine's two congressional districts and Nebraska's three, with Maine and Nebraska statewide forecasts mostly the sum of district forecasts but also informed by statewide polls. Electoral College ties of 269-269 are reported as ties in 2020 rather than broken. Faithless electors are not modeled.
findings.evidence_quote: In total, the model calculates a forecast in 54 jurisdictions

findings.statement: A 'major' third-party candidate, modeled explicitly as with Gary Johnson in 2016 or Perot in backtests, must be on the ballot almost everywhere, included in most polls, and usually polling in the mid-to-high single digits. 'Other' votes are predicted per state from the number of third-party candidates on the ballot, write-in rules, historical third-party share and competitiveness, since swing states give third parties fewer votes.
findings.evidence_quote: We defined major as (i) a candidate who is on the ballot almost everywhere, (ii) who is included in most polls and (iii) who usually polls in at least the mid-to-high single digits.

findings.statement: The model forecasts the vote as cast, assuming reasonable efforts to let eligible citizens vote and count legal ballots and that electors go to each state's popular-vote winner; it does not model extraconstitutional interference. Its probabilities can still serve as a benchmark for suspicious claims, such as a candidate claiming a state where it gave them 0.4 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: It does not account for the possibility of extraconstitutional shenanigans by Trump or by anyone else

findings.statement: FiveThirtyEight reports its models, including election forecasts since 2008, have been well calibrated over time, and its 2016 forecast gave Trump about 30 percent, higher than other models and markets, partly by detecting his potential Electoral College overperformance.
findings.evidence_quote: Candidates who our models claim have a 30 percent chance of winning really do win their races about 30 percent of the time

political_insights.insight: Greater polarization produces closer margins and smaller effects of the economy and incumbency.
political_insights.evidence: Fit across elections with roll-call polarization data.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Scale economic and incumbency effects down with polarization.

open_questions: Value of the drift constant and the scaling of the uncertainty index.
Exact ensemble weights for the rigid, demographic and regional methods.
Formula for poll-versus-ensemble weight as a function of poll volume and recency.
Functional form of the fundamentals regression combining economic index, incumbency and polarization.
